title: Build a System Explanation Readers Can Explore and Check Against Source
summary:
An architecture diagram can show a handler, an authorization service, and a renderer. A new engineer tracing a failed document preview still needs to know which path applies, where access is denied, and which source lines support the explanation.

A useful explanation should let the reader follow that question without losing the connection to the implementation. Living Explainers explores this idea through an authored model that generates a self-contained HTML page.

Start with a request path

The bundled example follows a document preview through validation, access review, and rendering. It contains three authored paths: success, denied access, and renderer timeout.

A reader can choose a path, inspect its steps, and look at source references and assumptions. A question about caller retries is explicitly outside the model's coverage. That boundary is useful: an explanation can show what it covers without inventing the behavior of the rest of the system.

The model distinguishes observed, documented, and proposed material. A proposed step should remain visibly proposed even if it sits beside a source-backed step in an attractive interface.

Generate the offline explorer

Use Python 3.11 or newer for the CLI. It needs no third-party runtime dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/asadani/living-explainers.git
cd living-explainers
out_dir="$(mktemp -d)"

python -m living_explainers validate fixtures/model.json \
  --root fixtures/system

python -m living_explainers check fixtures/model.json \
  --root fixtures/system --out "$out_dir/freshness.json"

python -m living_explainers build fixtures/model.json \
  --root fixtures/system --out "$out_dir/explorer.html"

The fixture validates as a model with five nodes and three paths. Its recorded source baselines are current, so the check exits successfully. Open explorer.html in a JavaScript-capable browser to explore it.

The output does not need a running application server. It contains a snapshot of the authored model and freshness information at build time. It does not fetch source files or monitor the repository after it has been exported.

Treat source changes as a review request

Source references retain file fingerprints and cited line ranges. A changed source can mark affected references stale; a missing file remains visible as missing. Material without a reviewed baseline remains unreviewed.

Running the renderer again cannot silently bless a new version of the source. Refreshing a baseline is an explicit review action after someone checks the referenced material.

This is conservative. The fingerprint covers the whole source file, so an unrelated edit can ask for review even if the explanation's cited behavior is unchanged. That creates maintenance work, but the alternative would require a stronger method for deciding which changes invalidate an explanation.

The distinction between building and reviewing is the design point: rendering an explanation and accepting its evidence are different operations.

An authored model still needs an author

Living Explainers does not infer architecture from a repository, execute the described system, or discover new failure behavior. Someone must choose the scope, write the steps, connect them to source, and review the claims.

That effort should earn its place. For a tiny function, a short explanation beside the code may be easier to maintain. A bounded request flow with multiple paths is a better candidate for an explorer because the reader has meaningful choices to inspect.

Visual polish also cannot establish teaching value. The current fixture demonstrates an interface and its maintenance mechanism; it does not establish that engineers learn faster with it.

Evaluate one concrete reader task

Choose a request that newcomers need to trace. Ask them to identify the access-denial boundary or the safest location for a change, using either the current documentation or the explorer. Record whether their answers are correct, which evidence they consult, and where the model leaves them uncertain.

Then change a referenced file and measure the author's maintenance effort. An explanation that helps readers today but is too costly to review next month may not be an improvement.

The MIT-licensed repository contains the request model, synthetic source fixture, renderer, and design plan.

title: Reviewing the Meaning Changes Hidden in a Rewrite
summary:
Compare these two sentences:

Guests must not reshare documents within 24 hours unless an owner approves the action.

Guests may reshare documents within 48 hours.

The second is shorter. It also changes the obligation, removes a negation, changes a quantity, and drops an approval condition. A request to simplify a specification can produce a cleaner sentence while changing what an engineer would implement.

A normal diff contains those edits. The difficulty is giving them attention amid punctuation fixes, reordered paragraphs, and other harmless revisions. Meaning Diff adds a focused review pass over a small set of literal patterns.

Give the reviewer a reason to stop

The tool compares two Markdown documents, aligns sentences, and reports changed quantities, obligation words, negations, condition suffixes, and added or dropped sentences. It retains the before and after text with source line numbers.

For the example above, a reviewer should investigate several independent questions:

Change Question for the reviewer
must becomes may Was the policy intentionally relaxed?
not disappears Did the permitted behavior reverse?
24 hours becomes 48 hours Was the time window intentionally changed?
The unless condition disappears Is owner approval still required anywhere?

The report does not answer those questions. It gives the reviewer located evidence for asking them.

Try it on the shipped specification

Use Python 3.11 or newer. There are no third-party runtime dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/asadani/meaning-diff.git
cd meaning-diff
out_dir="$(mktemp -d)"

python -m meaning_diff compare \
  fixtures/sharing-before.md fixtures/sharing-after.md \
  --format markdown --out "$out_dir/review.md"

python -m meaning_diff compare \
  fixtures/sharing-before.md fixtures/sharing-after.md \
  --format json --out "$out_dir/review.json"

Both comparison commands exit with status 1 because the fixture produces review signals. That exit status is an expected result, not an operational failure. Status 2 is reserved for problems such as invalid input or an unreadable file.

The fixture yields five changed sentence pairs and seven signals. It also includes a harmless paraphrase that appears as a changed pair without a configured signal. Exact unchanged sentences are omitted, and fenced code is excluded from prose comparison.

Sentence alignment is a design choice

Meaning Diff uses normalized exact matches as anchors. Within replacement blocks, it uses lexical similarity to pair remaining sentences. The alignment threshold is configurable; the default is 0.45.

That approach makes the implementation inspectable, but it also creates failure modes. A large paraphrase may not align with its predecessor. Similar wording can join unrelated sentences. Unmatched text remains visible as additions and drops, and the report retains the alignment method and scores so a reviewer can inspect suspicious pairs.

A signal's priority is a fixed hint about review order. It is not a measured probability of harm. A changed number can be an intentional correction; a seemingly harmless paraphrase can introduce a subtle policy error outside the detector's patterns.

Add a focused pass to the existing review

This is useful when a document contains obligations, limits, or conditional behavior: requirements, operational procedures, or internal policies. Keep the full diff and source documents available. Use the focused report to inspect changes that could alter an action or expectation.

For a practical evaluation, take a few realistic revisions and label the changes that a reviewer should notice. Compare ordinary diff review with diff plus the report. Record missed consequential edits and irrelevant flags, as well as the effort of reading the extra output.

The project has not established an accuracy rate on a labeled real-world corpus. Its current contribution is a small, reproducible way to surface specific patterns without asking another model to declare that the rewrite preserved meaning.

The MIT-licensed source includes the report schema, fixture revisions, and the comparison algorithm.

title: What if your AI didn't have to start over every morning?
summary:
If you worked beside someone every day, and every morning they walked in with no memory of yesterday, how long would it take before you stopped treating them like a partner and started treating them like a tool?

That's the relationship most of us have with our AI assistants right now. We spend an afternoon with Claude working through a tricky refactor. We agree on an approach, rule out two dead ends, and learn that one config file must never be touched. Then the session ends. The next morning we open a new one, and it's a stranger again. Friendly, capable, and completely blank.

So we start the day by re-explaining. Where we left off. What we decided. What we already tried. It's a small tax, but we pay it every single session, and it adds up.

Why this matters more than it looks

Think about a night-shift nurse handing off to the day shift. Nobody expects the day nurse to remember the night. What they get is a good handoff: what happened, what's still open, what to watch out for. The handoff is what lets care continue even though the people change.

Our AI sessions have no handoff. Each one starts cold.

I wanted to know how bad that really was, so I measured it. Over 43 of my own sessions across six weeks this spring, I logged every time the assistant needed something it should have known but didn't. That could be a lookup after it had "oriented," a "we already tried that" from me, or the assistant admitting it was missing something. Only 33% of sessions started clean. 26% had five or more misses. That's 173 misses in all.

To be fair about it, this is one person's setup, and it was already a fairly mature memory system. It's n=1, not a benchmark. The full write-up is in the repo if you want to poke at it. But it matched what I felt every day: the assistant could find things when asked, yet it often didn't know what it was missing.

That's the distinction Rekindle is built around. Storing memories is one problem. Showing up oriented is a different one.

What Rekindle does

Rekindle is a small open-source MCP server and CLI. It runs entirely on your machine, on a local SQLite file. It has no API keys and no network calls. It works in three moments.

At the end of a session, the assistant calls end_session and writes a structured handoff. The fields are a checkpoint (required), decisions, open loops, constraints, warnings, preferences, what changed in the working relationship, and where to pick up next. It's more than a summary. It's a note to the next shift.

At the start of the next session, the boot_report tool builds an orientation report. It reads your identity notes and the last checkpoint, lists open loops, flags gaps (missing identity, empty categories, stale data), and gives a simple 0–100 score so you can see at a glance how oriented the assistant is. In Claude Code, an opt-in SessionStart hook can also deliver a budgeted orientation packet automatically at startup, resume, /clear and /compact, so the model doesn't have to be asked.

In the long middle, an opt-in PreCompact hook saves a copy of recent conversation before Claude Code compacts the context. You can read it back later as a summary, a structured view, or the raw transcript excerpt.

Between those moments there are plain memory tools too: store_memory, search_memory (full-text, BM25-ranked and weighted by importance), list_memories, update_memory and delete_memory, plus list_captures, read_capture and capture_now for the compaction captures. That's 10 tools in all.

Quick start

You need Node.js 22 or newer.

# in your project
npx rekindle init

# register the server with Claude Code
claude mcp add rekindle -- npx -y rekindle

# optional: save context before compaction
npx rekindle setup-hooks

# optional: deliver the orientation packet at every session start
npx rekindle setup-delivery

init creates a local .rekindle/ folder (database and an identity template) and keeps it out of git. Neither hook is installed unless you ask for it. Then fill in .rekindle/identity.md and paste the boot instructions that init prints into your CLAUDE.md.

If you want one memory across every project, npx rekindle init --global sets things up in your home directory, and the hooks then go in your user-level Claude Code settings. Pair it with claude mcp add --scope user rekindle -- npx -y rekindle. Cursor and Claude Desktop work too, with the usual mcpServers JSON entry. The README has the snippets.

What it doesn't do (yet)

I'd rather you hear the limits from me than find them the hard way.

  • The automatic packet is lean. The SessionStart hook delivers your identity notes and the last checkpoint. Open loops and recent captures show up when the assistant calls boot_report, not in the automatic packet. Some handoff fields, like next focus, constraints and warnings, are stored but only come back if someone searches for them. Closing that gap is my top priority.
  • The score is a checklist, not a judgment. It checks that things exist. It doesn't check that they're fresh or true. A months-old checkpoint scores the same as last night's.
  • Compaction captures are mostly the raw tail. The "structured" view is a placeholder until it's reviewed, so the value today is the saved transcript itself.
  • No semantic search. It's keyword search with good ranking. Embeddings are on the roadmap.
  • It's not a vault. The SQLite file isn't encrypted, and boot_report reads local paths you give it. Use disk encryption if that matters to you, and only connect clients you trust. Don't enable transcript capture in sessions that handle secrets.
  • Coverage varies by client. Session-start delivery is measured on Claude Code (macOS, Windows), Claude Desktop's Code surface, and Cursor via hooks. On Linux the hook path is the same, but I haven't finished measuring delivery there yet. Claude Desktop's chat surface has no hooks, so it's tools only.
  • It's young. v0.4.1 has 568 tests running in CI on Node 22, 24 and 26. It's still one maintainer's project.

Why I keep building it

Here's where I've landed. A tool you have to re-introduce yourself to every day stays a tool. A partner remembers what you were doing together, what you promised each other, and what not to break. Continuity is the line between the two.

Rekindle won't make an AI remember the way we do. What it can do is make sure each new session starts with an honest handoff, and with a clear list of what it doesn't know. That's a small step, but I think it's the right first one toward giving people the gift of an AI partnership instead of just a tool.

If you try it, I'd love to hear two things: what a good handoff should contain, and whether the score helps you or just adds noise.

Repo: https://github.com/Skitchy/rekindle (MIT) · npm: rekindle

— Skitch

title: Finding the processes Claude Code leaves running on Windows
summary:
A scan of my machine, 38 hours after boot, found a next dev server that had held port 3001 for 35 hours with nothing connected to it. An ng serve had sat idle for 11 hours. Around them were 20 bare tail.exe, grep.exe and sh.exe rows in Task Manager, with nothing to say which project they belonged to.

All of them came from my Claude Code sessions: dev servers, tail -f watchers on task output files, small scripts. The sessions had ended and the processes kept running. There's an upstream issue about it, #62659, and a bot closed it as not planned.

So I wrote Sweepling, a Windows tray app that notices these leftovers and closes them once you confirm.

Why this is a Windows problem

On Linux an orphan is adopted by init or a subreaper, and a cleanup tool can end a whole process group in one call. cc-reaper does this well on macOS and Linux.

Windows does neither. When a parent exits, its children keep running and keep the dead parent's PID in their own process record. Windows also reuses PIDs, so a few minutes later that number can belong to something unrelated. Task Manager's tree only nests a process under a parent that's still alive, so an orphan shows up as one more top-level node.exe.

That gives the first rule: a process's parent is gone when its PID is missing, or when that PID now belongs to a process that started after the child.

Proc? ParentOf(Proc p) =>
    p.ParentPid != p.Pid
    && byPid.TryGetValue(p.ParentPid, out var parent)
    && parent.Started <= p.Started ? parent : null;

You can run the same check in PowerShell without installing anything:

$all = Get-CimInstance Win32_Process
$byId = @{}; $all | ForEach-Object { $byId[$_.ProcessId] = $_ }
$all | Where-Object { $p = $byId[$_.ParentProcessId]; -not $p -or $p.CreationDate -gt $_.CreationDate } |
  Where-Object Name -in 'node.exe', 'tail.exe', 'grep.exe', 'bash.exe', 'sh.exe' |
  Select-Object ProcessId, Name, CreationDate

It will also list orphans that have nothing to do with Claude Code. Telling those apart is the hard part.

Tying an orphan to a session

Plenty of programs start a helper and exit on purpose, so an orphan on its own isn't a leftover. Sweepling only offers a process it can tie to a Claude Code session, and it has three ways to do that, strongest first.

  1. The family tree. Every few seconds Sweepling takes a snapshot of your processes and records which session each one descends from. Ancestry is only visible while the parents are alive, so it learns early and keeps what it learned after a parent exits.
  2. CLAUDE_PID. Claude Code puts its own PID in its children's environment. Sweepling reads another process's environment from its PEB. That memory belongs to the other process, so every size and pointer in it is treated as untrusted and every read is bounded.
  3. Command-line rules. Programs run from Git Bash are the awkward case: an MSYS2 process hands Windows only a handful of environment variables, and CLAUDE_PID isn't one of them. For those, a small rules file matches things like a grep --line-buffered from Git Bash's folder, or a command line that points into Claude Code's temp folder.

When Sweepling can't tell whether a session has ended, it treats the session as running. A wrong "running" only delays an offer. A wrong "ended" offers someone's live work.

Strays that share one dead parent and started within ten seconds of each other become a group, together with everything under them, and you close a group as one.

Is it still in use?

Belonging to an ended session still isn't enough. A group waits until its parent has been gone for a minute, and it's never offered when:

title: SuperTuxKart took down its online services due to a serious threat
summary:
SuperTuxKart and other major platforms took systems offline following exploit attempts tied to PHP2Shell.

The project is entirely rebuilding its server in Python without AI assistance, expecting a full security audit before migrating existing accounts.

The threat, known as PHP2Shell, has also led other organizations, including Wikimedia, DeviantArt, and government websites, to shut down their systems for security reasons. According to the game's creators, attack attempts were recorded on October 17, four days before the problem was publicly known.

Although the game's mainframe was not compromised, the team decided to shut it down as a precaution. The system was found to be running an older version of the code, and a security firm that reviewed the situation recommended that it be rewritten from scratch rather than being put back into service.

What affects the closure?

Due to the outage, players are temporarily unable to:

READ ALSO

Ukraine's military satellite internet restored after restrictions

  • change their account passwords,
  • check the scores,
  • upload new additions.

On the other hand, local functions such as playing on the same screen, connections between nearby computers, and file downloads for those who already have an account continue to function normally.

Next steps and fundraising

The game's developers decided to rebuild the system from scratch using a different programming language, without the help of artificial intelligence. The new version is expected to take several weeks to complete, and will undergo a rigorous security review before accounts can be transferred.

To help complete the effort, the creators started a fundraiser with a goal of $4.000. A security company agreed to double the effort by offering equivalent hours of technical work.

Finally, the creators recommend that those who have used the same password on other services change it immediately.

title: How a peak finder decides which mountains you can see, and what I measured
summary:
I wanted a peak finder whose method I can read, change and host myself. So I built WhichPeak, a static web app that draws a labeled 360 degree panorama from open elevation tiles.

What it does

You open a link or drop a pin. WhichPeak reads AWS Terrain Tiles, builds the terrain in six rings of detail from 5 km out to 1000 km, and draws the view. It adds earth curvature and refraction, shades the terrain with the real sun for the hour you pick, and labels each summit that is actually above the horizon. Click a label for elevation, distance, bearing, the angle above the horizon and how far the peak clears the terrain in front of it.

There is also a line of sight tool that plots the profile between two points and names the ridge that blocks it.

How the horizon works

For each pixel column the renderer sweeps outward and keeps the highest slope it has seen. Curvature drops the ground by d squared over twice the effective radius, and refraction enlarges that radius by 1 over (1 minus k) with k set to 0.13. A peak gets a label only if its own slope beats the sweep. The known flaw is a smear in the foreground on very steep ground. It is cosmetic and does not touch the labels.

What I measured

The terrain for a 150 km view from the Gornergrat is drawn in 4.6 s, the median of six cold runs in headless Chrome over the real network. At 400 km it is 6.6 s. Peak names come from Overpass and load separately, between 10 and 32 s in my runs. A bundled list of 35,621 summits above 1800 m fills in when no mirror answers.

I also tested the line of sight against sightlines that people documented. Pic de Finestrelles to Pic Gaspard, 443 km, comes out blocked by 48 m at the average refraction and visible from k = 0.145. That matches a photograph taken in 2016 under strong refraction. Marys Peak to Mount Rainier, 295.8 km, is visible with 78 m of clearance.

Photo mode is experimental. I ran eight casual photos with the place set and no heading. One matched and seven were flagged as weak matches. Nothing was reported as matched when it was wrong.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/Arthur031221/WhichPeak.git
cd WhichPeak
npm install
npm run dev

The live demo is at https://arthur031221.github.io/WhichPeak/ and the code is at https://github.com/Arthur031221/WhichPeak. The interface comes in nine languages and the project has 93 unit tests and 10 browser tests. I built it with help from AI coding assistants.

Which long sightline should I test next?

title: 7 Project Management Tools for Freelancers, Compared on Price and Free-Plan Limits
summary:
Choosing project management software sounds simple until you compare the actual limits. One platform is excellent for a solo freelancer but expensive for a growing agency. Another offers dozens of features but takes too long to set up. A third looks simple at first, then needs paid upgrades the moment you want timelines, automation, or better reporting.
I compared seven tools with freelancer needs in mind rather than enterprise checklists: ClickUp, Trello, Asana, Notion, monday.com, Bonsai, and Jira. Here is what actually decides the choice.
The verdict up front
ClickUp is the strongest overall choice when you want tasks, time tracking, documents, dashboards, and project planning in one place. Trello is the better choice if you want a simple visual workflow and nothing more. Asana is the strong option for structured client work with dependencies and approvals. Notion is the pick when project work and documentation need to live together. monday.com fits small teams that prefer highly visual workflows. Bonsai is the one to look at when you want project management connected to proposals, contracts, invoices, and payments. Jira is for software development teams running Agile workflows, and it is usually more complexity than a designer or writer needs.
Free plans: read the limits, not the word "free"
Free is where most freelancers start, and the limits are wildly different.
ClickUp's free plan includes unlimited members and unlimited tasks, which sounds unbeatable until you hit the 60 MB storage limit. Trello's free plan gives you up to 10 boards and 10 collaborators per workspace, with unlimited cards. Asana's free Personal plan is limited to two users, which is fine for a solo freelancer with one collaborator and a wall for anyone else. Notion's free plan is built for individuals. monday.com's free plan is two seats and three boards. Jira's free plan supports up to 10 users, which is generous if you are on a dev team.
The point is not that one free plan is best. It is that the limit that bites you depends on how you work. If you store a lot of files, ClickUp's storage cap matters. If you juggle ten clients, Trello's board limit matters. If you work with a small team, Asana's two-user cap matters on day one.
What you actually pay
For a small team of three, the per-user math looks like this. ClickUp Unlimited at $7 per user per month billed annually is about $21 a month. Trello Standard at $5 per user per month is about $15. Asana Starter is $10.99 per user per month, and one detail is easy to miss: Asana does not offer a one-user paid subscription, its paid plans start with tiered seat options. Notion Plus is $10 per member per month and Business is $20. Bonsai Basic is $9 per user per month, Essentials $19, and Premium $29. Jira Standard is $7.91 per user per month and Premium is $14.54.
Pricing changes often, so treat these as the figures checked in 2026 and confirm the current plan before you buy. The pattern is what matters: the cheapest starting price is not always the cheapest solution once you count the extra tools, the manual work, and the future upgrades.
The mistake most freelancers make
The most common mistake is paying for complexity you will not touch. A solo freelancer with a list of tasks and a few deadlines does not need Gantt charts, workload management, and portfolio reporting. Trello or a simple board will do, and you will actually use it every day. The other mistake is the opposite one: picking a simple board for a five-person agency, then outgrowing it in three months and paying the migration cost in lost time.
Start with the simplest platform that covers your current workflow. You can always move to a more detailed system when the work actually requires it. The best project management software is not the one with the most features. It is the one your team will actually open every day.
For the full comparison with the per-tool breakdowns, the pricing tables at different list sizes, and the FAQ section, the complete guide is here: 7 Best Project Management Software for Freelancers (2026)

title: Rotifer v0.9.3: Genes scored against the season, run with the permissions they declare (npm 0.30.0)
summary:
v0.9.3 changes two things about how a gene is judged and how it runs.

  • Judged against its season. Arena F(g) used to measure a gene's speed and cost against fixed constants. It now compares them with the season median of genes in the same domain and fidelity.
  • Run as declared. Every CLI path now runs a gene with exactly the permissions its phenotype declares. Only a Hybrid gene that declares network access can reach the network, and each of its requests is checked before it leaves the sandbox.

v0.9.3 is the protocol version. It shipped in @rotifer/playground 0.30.0 on 2026-10-21. Install 0.30.1, the security patch that followed.

F(g) against the season

F(g) has two efficiency terms: how fast a gene ran and how much it cost. Each is scored relative to a reference: L_ref for latency, Cost_ref for resource cost. Until now both references were fixed numbers, the same for a text formatter and a web search.

rotifer arena submit now asks the Registry for the current season's median among genes in the same domain and the same fidelity, and scores against that. It prints which reference it used. When there is a median:

Reference scale: season  median of   /  genes (L_ref … ms, Cost_ref … fuel)

When fewer than 5 such genes have measured runs, there is not enough to take a median from, and it falls back to the fixed constants and says why:

Reference scale: fixed constants — too few measured  /  genes this season for a median

Two smaller changes feed the same pool of data:

  • Estimated submissions upload their measured runs too. Before, only some submissions contributed runs, so medians had less to work with.
  • Submitting a gene again updates its Arena row instead of failing.

What has not changed: scores are still marked estimated and stay out of the ranking. F(g) also has coverage and robustness terms, and those are not measured yet. Until they are, a season-relative score is a better estimate, not a verdict.

Genes run with the permissions they declare

Every CLI path that executes a gene (agent run, run, test, arena submit and the publish gate) used to hand the sandbox the same default permission set for every gene. That default refused the network to all of them, including genes that declare it.

Now each gene runs with exactly what its phenotype declares:

  • A Hybrid gene with a network block can reach the domains it lists, through rotifer.net, and nothing else.
  • Native and Wrapped genes get no network, even if they carry a network block. A request from one of them is refused at the sandbox boundary.
  • In a composition, each gene gets its own set. A Hybrid gene running next to a Native one can reach its domains; the Native one still cannot.

Outbound requests are checked, and billed separately

A gene's fuel counts instructions inside the WASM sandbox. A network request is mostly time spent outside it, so it is metered separately: each request carries a surcharge.

In 0.30.0:

  • Before each request is sent, the sandbox checks the request count, the time already spent in host calls, and the run's deadline. If any limit would be exceeded, the request is not sent.
  • The surcharge is billed to resource_cost, not to the gene's fuel. Previously one successful request could use up more fuel than a whole CLI run allows, so the gene got its response and then failed for running out of fuel. Now the response arrives and the run continues. The cost still shows up in resource_cost, which is what F(g)'s cost term reads, so moving work into network calls does not make a gene look cheaper.

Also in this release

  • Two fixes: the genome snapshot after agent run counts a compiled Native gene as executable, and genome import only suggests dropping --pinned when you passed it.
  • 0.30.1 followed on 2026-10-24. It moves the plugin and Skills to MCP server 0.19.4, updates dependencies for security advisories, and comes with server-side Arena and account changes.

The full list is in the changelog.

Where this sits

Genes that compete on merit are the goal. This release makes the comparison fairer, because a gene is now measured against its peers in the current season, and makes execution stricter, because a gene can only do what it declared.

Not in this release:

  • Scores still stay estimated and are not ranked.
  • There is no Cloud execution endpoint or Petri hookup yet; both come in a later release. For now, genes run on your machine through the CLI.
  • Native and Wrapped genes cannot reach the network at all. A gene that needs to call an outside service has to be Hybrid and declare where it goes.
  • Genes written in TypeScript cannot call rotifer.net yet. For now, a Hybrid gene that goes online has to be compiled to WASM that imports the host functions directly.

Install / Upgrade 

npm install -g @rotifer/playground@0.30.1

This article was originally published on rotifer.dev. Follow the project on GitHub or install the CLI: npm i -g @rotifer/playground.

v0.9.3 is the protocol version. It shipped in @rotifer/playground 0.30.0 on 2026-10-21. Install 0.30.1, the security patch that followed.

F(g) against the season

F(g) has two efficiency terms: how fast a gene ran and how much it cost. Each is scored relative to a reference: L_ref for latency, Cost_ref for resource cost. Until now both references were fixed numbers, the same for a text formatter and a web search.

rotifer arena submit now asks the Registry for the current season's median among genes in the same domain and the same fidelity, and scores against that. It prints which reference it used. When there is a median:

Reference scale: season  median of   /  genes (L_ref … ms, Cost_ref … fuel)

When fewer than 5 such genes have measured runs, there is not enough to take a median from, and it falls back to the fixed constants and says why:

Reference scale: fixed constants — too few measured  /  genes this season for a median

Two smaller changes feed the same pool of data:

  • Estimated submissions upload their measured runs too. Before, only some submissions contributed runs, so medians had less to work with.
  • Submitting a gene again updates its Arena row instead of failing.

What has not changed: scores are still marked estimated and stay out of the ranking. F(g) also has coverage and robustness terms, and those are not measured yet. Until they are, a season-relative score is a better estimate, not a verdict.

Genes run with the permissions they declare

Every CLI path that executes a gene (agent run, run, test, arena submit and the publish gate) used to hand the sandbox the same default permission set for every gene. That default refused the network to all of them, including genes that declare it.

Now each gene runs with exactly what its phenotype declares:

  • A Hybrid gene with a network block can reach the domains it lists, through rotifer.net, and nothing else.
  • Native and Wrapped genes get no network, even if they carry a network block. A request from one of them is refused at the sandbox boundary.
  • In a composition, each gene gets its own set. A Hybrid gene running next to a Native one can reach its domains; the Native one still cannot.

Outbound requests are checked, and billed separately

A gene's fuel counts instructions inside the WASM sandbox. A network request is mostly time spent outside it, so it is metered separately: each request carries a surcharge.

In 0.30.0:

  • Before each request is sent, the sandbox checks the request count, the time already spent in host calls, and the run's deadline. If any limit would be exceeded, the request is not sent.
  • The surcharge is billed to resource_cost, not to the gene's fuel. Previously one successful request could use up more fuel than a whole CLI run allows, so the gene got its response and then failed for running out of fuel. Now the response arrives and the run continues. The cost still shows up in resource_cost, which is what F(g)'s cost term reads, so moving work into network calls does not make a gene look cheaper.

  • Two fixes: the genome snapshot after agent run counts a compiled Native gene as executable, and genome import only suggests dropping --pinned when you passed it.
  • 0.30.1 followed on 2026-10-24. It moves the plugin and Skills to MCP server 0.19.4, updates dependencies for security advisories, and comes with server-side Arena and account changes.

The full list is in the changelog.

Where this sits

Genes that compete on merit are the goal. This release makes the comparison fairer, because a gene is now measured against its peers in the current season, and makes execution stricter, because a gene can only do what it declared.

Not in this release:

  • Scores still stay estimated and are not ranked.
  • There is no Cloud execution endpoint or Petri hookup yet; both come in a later release. For now, genes run on your machine through the CLI.
  • Native and Wrapped genes cannot reach the network at all. A gene that needs to call an outside service has to be Hybrid and declare where it goes.
  • Genes written in TypeScript cannot call rotifer.net yet. For now, a Hybrid gene that goes online has to be compiled to WASM that imports the host functions directly.

title: I run a dozen Claude Code sessions at once. This tmux console tells me which one needs me
summary:
TL;DR — claude-tmux-sessions is a small set of tmux tools for running many Claude Code sessions in parallel. It answers three questions I kept asking myself: which session is waiting on me, what is everyone doing, and what do I do when one account runs out of quota? MIT, tmux + bash + python3, driven by Claude Code hooks.

How I use Claude Code

Some context first, or the design will look odd.

I use two Claude accounts to push several projects forward at the same time:

  • One account per project. Each account has a 5-hour and a 7-day usage window. If one busy project shares an account with the others, it stalls them too. With an account per project, each has its own quota.
  • One session per role inside an account. Algorithms, backend, frontend, testing: one session each, so each context holds only its own part of the work and doesn't drift.
  • I only make decisions. I don't watch any one terminal. I go over when a session needs a yes/no, or when it has finished and I should look at the result.
  • Memory lives in files. Project rules, hand-off notes and a dev log are in the repository, so switching accounts or sessions loses nothing.

That adds up to a lot of sessions open at once, more than one person can watch. tmux only manages windows; it has no idea what the Claude inside each window is doing. Hence this.

Four pieces

Status bar: who is waiting on you

Each session reports its state through Claude Code hooks, and the status bar counts them:

  • ⏸ waiting for your confirmation (a permission prompt is open and Claude is idle) — the only state that rings and sends a notification;
  • ✔ finished, and you haven't looked yet;
  • ▶ running, nothing to do;
  • ✓ finished, and you've seen it.

The four counts never move: a zero turns grey but keeps its place, so you can click from muscle memory. Click ⏸ to jump to the session that has waited longest; click ✔ to get a list of just the finished-but-unread ones:

That list is a tmux 3.7 floating pane, not display-popup, which is why clicking anywhere outside closes it — display-popup swallows clicks outside its box.

Picker: what is everyone doing

prefix + g lists every session, grouped by tmux session (for me, one per project), with a live view of the one under the cursor. Every row is numbered; type the number to jump. It behaves like an inbox: visiting a session marks it read, and quiet ones fold away by default, so the list shows only what needs you.

Sidebar: everything about this one session

Every Claude gets a sidebar on its right that is about this session only:

  • Every turn. What you said and the start of the reply. Click a turn and the main pane scrolls to that turn's final answer. Turns before a /compact fold into one line. It reads the transcript file, not the screen.
  • Quota. Context, 5-hour and 7-day bars. Grey until something runs well ahead of an even pace.
  • Buttons. git (with the count of uncommitted files), files, refresh quota, switch account, close.

The git and files buttons open lazygit and yazi floating over the right 60 % of the window, so the Claude on the left doesn't re-wrap; click outside and they're gone:

Rule of thumb: global things go on the status bar, things about the current session go on the sidebar. The status bar is short on space, and this keeps both uncluttered.

Switch accounts: keep going when one runs out

Click ⇄ on the sidebar and the session exits, then comes back as claude --resume of the same session id under the other account. Same conversation, same context. There are guard rails: a session that is working is left alone; one with unsent text in its prompt is left alone (exiting would lose it); a window with agent-team teammates first gets a line typed to the lead asking it to wind the team down, and switches once they've exited.

Trade-offs I made on purpose

  • Hooks, not screen scraping, for state. Sessions report their own state when it changes: accurate, no polling, no CPU. The screen is read only where there is no other way ("which turn is where", "is there unsent text").
  • An inbox, not a dashboard. Things you've seen turn ✓ on their own and come back when that session does something new. Nobody maintains the list.
  • Everything is clickable. I work mostly by voice and trackpad, so every segment and button takes a click. Keyboard shortcuts are there too.
  • When in doubt, don't switch accounts. It skips and tells you why rather than risk losing anything.

The rest of my setup

The tmux console is one of four pieces. I also dictate almost every prompt with a push-to-talk voice tool (an LLM proofreads each transcript, and Claude adds the words it sees misheard to the vocabulary itself), and look back at usage and configuration in a local web dashboard. That's written up in docs/workbench.md.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/threedaycat/claude-tmux-sessions.git ~/projects/claude-tmux-sessions
~/projects/claude-tmux-sessions/install.sh --lang en

Then add one line to your tmux config, source-file ~/projects/claude-tmux-sessions/tmux/claude-tmux.conf, and put the status-bar segments into your own status line; the README walks through it.

Known limits, up front: I use it daily on macOS only (Linux is untested); you need a Nerd Font for the icons; and a few features read Claude Code's screen, so a Claude Code UI change may need a follow-up fix. Issues and PRs welcome.

  • ⏸ waiting for your confirmation (a permission prompt is open and Claude is idle) — the only state that rings and sends a notification;
  • ✔ finished, and you haven't looked yet;
  • ▶ running, nothing to do;
  • ✓ finished, and you've seen it.

The four counts never move: a zero turns grey but keeps its place, so you can click from muscle memory. Click ⏸ to jump to the session that has waited longest; click ✔ to get a list of just the finished-but-unread ones:

That list is a tmux 3.7 floating pane, not display-popup, which is why clicking anywhere outside closes it — display-popup swallows clicks outside its box.

Picker: what is everyone doing

prefix + g lists every session, grouped by tmux session (for me, one per project), with a live view of the one under the cursor. Every row is numbered; type the number to jump. It behaves like an inbox: visiting a session marks it read, and quiet ones fold away by default, so the list shows only what needs you.

Sidebar: everything about this one session

Every Claude gets a sidebar on its right that is about this session only:

  • Every turn. What you said and the start of the reply. Click a turn and the main pane scrolls to that turn's final answer. Turns before a /compact fold into one line. It reads the transcript file, not the screen.
  • Quota. Context, 5-hour and 7-day bars. Grey until something runs well ahead of an even pace.
  • Buttons. git (with the count of uncommitted files), files, refresh quota, switch account, close.

The git and files buttons open lazygit and yazi floating over the right 60 % of the window, so the Claude on the left doesn't re-wrap; click outside and they're gone:

Rule of thumb: global things go on the status bar, things about the current session go on the sidebar. The status bar is short on space, and this keeps both uncluttered.

Switch accounts: keep going when one runs out

Click ⇄ on the sidebar and the session exits, then comes back as claude --resume of the same session id under the other account. Same conversation, same context. There are guard rails: a session that is working is left alone; one with unsent text in its prompt is left alone (exiting would lose it); a window with agent-team teammates first gets a line typed to the lead asking it to wind the team down, and switches once they've exited.

Trade-offs I made on purpose

  • Hooks, not screen scraping, for state. Sessions report their own state when it changes: accurate, no polling, no CPU. The screen is read only where there is no other way ("which turn is where", "is there unsent text").
  • An inbox, not a dashboard. Things you've seen turn ✓ on their own and come back when that session does something new. Nobody maintains the list.
  • Everything is clickable. I work mostly by voice and trackpad, so every segment and button takes a click. Keyboard shortcuts are there too.
  • When in doubt, don't switch accounts. It skips and tells you why rather than risk losing anything.

The rest of my setup

The tmux console is one of four pieces. I also dictate almost every prompt with a push-to-talk voice tool (an LLM proofreads each transcript, and Claude adds the words it sees misheard to the vocabulary itself), and look back at usage and configuration in a local web dashboard. That's written up in docs/workbench.md.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/threedaycat/claude-tmux-sessions.git ~/projects/claude-tmux-sessions
~/projects/claude-tmux-sessions/install.sh --lang en

Then add one line to your tmux config, source-file ~/projects/claude-tmux-sessions/tmux/claude-tmux.conf, and put the status-bar segments into your own status line; the README walks through it.

Known limits, up front: I use it daily on macOS only (Linux is untested); you need a Nerd Font for the icons; and a few features read Claude Code's screen, so a Claude Code UI change may need a follow-up fix. Issues and PRs welcome.

title: We showed 8 real Facebook ads to 120 simulated buyers. It ranked them backwards, and still found the leak.
summary:
Simulation tools love to show the run where they were right. This is a run where one was wrong, and why it was still worth doing.

The setup

csca.ai sells prep for the CSCA exam (the test for studying in China) to students and parents in South and Southeast Asia. They ran 11 Facebook ads for a free mock test across Nepal, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Vietnam and Sri Lanka, and let us use the real results.

Real results (Meta Ads Manager): $56.05 spent, 274,557 impressions, 4,466 clicks, 1,500 landing page views, 16 sign-ups.

Then we gave MarketMirror the 8 that got most of the budget, plus a brief, without the results. It built 120 simulated students and parents (8 audiences × 15 people, each with a short life interview), put the ads in realistic Facebook feeds three times over with different random seeds, and ran a survey on the sign-up offer.

Where it was wrong: clicks

We compared the simulated click ranking with the real one. Rank correlation: -0.84. That's not "a bit off", that's almost backwards. The simulation's favourite ad was the Nepal broad audience; the real winner was the Indonesia parents ad at 2.32% CTR.

If you'd used it to pick which ad gets the budget, it would have pointed you the wrong way. We'd rather say that out loud than hide the run.

Where it was right: the leak

Look at the real funnel again: 1,500 people reached the page and 16 signed up. About 1 in 100.

The simulated buyers had already said why, in their own words and their own languages:

"Gratis tapi minta password lagi? Jangan." (Free, but asking for a password again? No way.) (Indonesia)

"Phone number dhele spam asbhe." (Give them my number and the spam starts.) (Bangladesh)

"Free sign-up? They want my phone and email. Harvesting data for sure." (Nepal)

In the survey, trust ("looks like a scam") was the top blocker for 56% of the simulated people, and privacy for 28%. The real sign-up form asks for full name, email, phone number, country and a password, for a free test.

The ad wasn't the main problem. The page after it was.

What it suggested next

From the real ad data plus the run, MarketMirror's ideas step wrote five next tests. Two of them:

  • Zero-friction entry: a 3-question quiz first, no email, no personal data.
  • Privacy-first page: say plainly how the data is used, cut the form to 3 fields.

These are proposals, not results. The point is the order: fix the page before buying more clicks.

What we take from it

  1. Don't use a simulation to rank ads by CTR. At least not until a backtest on your own past ads says it can. (MarketMirror has backtest and calibrate for exactly this.)
  2. Do use it to find the "why". Objections, in buyers' own words, by audience, before you spend.
  3. Real data in, next test out. The useful loop is: export real results → compare → test the fix on simulated buyers → run the small real test.

Try it

MarketMirror is open source (AGPL-3.0) and runs from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini or any MCP agent.

👉 https://github.com/DarkWorldCoder/market-mirror: if it saves you one bad launch, a ⭐ helps other people find it.

title: I highlight paper books. A small open model types my quotes while I sleep
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What I Built

I read on paper, with a highlighter in hand. Every quote that stops me ends up in a Notion database: knowing I'll keep what I mark makes me read more carefully, writing it down helps me remember it, and later I can find the right line when it comes up in a conversation or in something I'm writing.

The chore is in between: sitting down with the book, finding each highlighted passage again and typing it word by word. By the end of a book I have dozens of highlighted lines and no will to copy them.

Dogear removes that chore. While reading, the only extra thing I do is take a photo of each page I highlighted. Overnight, a small open-weight model running on a plain CPU in the cloud reads the photos and pulls out exactly the highlighted passages. In the morning I review them and stay in full control: I can keep, edit or delete any quote, and add one the night run missed. What I keep stays in my library, and a Notion export is next.

Dogear works end to end today: I photograph a page from the app, the night run reads it, and the quotes wait for me in the morning. What's still ahead lists what comes next.

Demo

Try it: dogear-web.onrender.com. Anyone can sign in and start their own library. Page photos are read by the next nightly run (06:00 UTC) and deleted afterwards.

The video walks through the whole loop with public-domain books. The screens are the real app with demo data, and the quotes and crops come from Dogear's own pipeline (Tesseract and Gemma 4 on a CPU) run on a page of Pride and Prejudice. The night-run numbers are a real line from the Render log.

Code

teofurlan / dogear

Dogear

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 3: Slow and Steady.

What it does

Reading on paper with a highlighter is great; copying the highlights out afterwards is not. Dogear moves that chore to a night job and keeps you in charge of the result:

  1. Add a book by typing it or photographing its cover. OCR suggests the title and author; nothing is saved until you confirm.
  2. Photograph each page you highlighted while the book is still open. The photo goes to a private bucket.
  3. Overnight, a cron job reads every pending page with Tesseract and Gemma 4 on a CPU, stores each highlighted passage as a…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

My highlighter is almost invisible to a computer

Before writing any app code, I tested the riskiest assumption with three real photos taken on my lap, one-handed. In a phone photo, a highlighter barely changes the paper: its color saturation measured about 7 out of 255, which is basically gray.

What worked was the Lab color space, which separates brightness from color. Instead of looking for a particular color, the code measures how far each pixel drifts from the paper's own tint, so it doesn't care which pen I picked. Light was the next trap: with half a page in shadow, one paper tint no longer fit the whole photo. The fix was to fit the tint as a smooth surface across the page and compare each pixel with the tint at its own position. That found every highlighted block on my test pages.

The model is a good reader and a bad judge

My first plan was to hand the whole photo to Gemma 4 (e4b, running in Ollama) and ask for the highlighted text. On one page it found 1 of 3 passages. On the other, it confidently returned the chapter title, which isn't highlighted at all. Given only a crop, it read well, but once it silently dropped a whole clause. A quote app that drops words is worse than no app.

So the design flipped: the model reads, the code decides.

  1. Color decides what is highlighted. It's deterministic and cheap.
  2. OCR finds where every word is. Tesseract returns a box for each word, and a word belongs to a quote when enough of the paper under it carries highlighter. That found the exact first and last word of every passage, even when a highlight starts mid-line.
  3. Two readers, compared. OCR knows where but misreads letters. Gemma writes clean text but can skip words. Each block is read by both, and Gemma's version is kept where they agree.
  4. Disagreement is flagged for me, with the photo crop next to the quote. Flags only point my attention: every quote stays mine to keep, edit or delete.

On my two test pages, the pipeline found 3 of 3 passages on each, with no false quotes. Watching Gemma fail taught me two fixes: send crops shaped like a text selection instead of scattered word boxes, and compare readings in a way that forgives OCR's glued words and the page's line-break hyphens. In the end, 4 of the 6 quotes came out with both readers agreeing, and the other 2 were flagged, exactly where OCR scrambled the text near the book's gutter. No wrong quote was presented as confident.

Slow on purpose

None of this has to happen when I take the photo, so it doesn't. A nightly cron job on Render processes the day's photos on a plain CPU, with no GPU. The model weights are baked into the Docker image, and a page takes about a minute and a half on four CPU cores, so even a heavy reading day of 30 pages is done in under an hour, long before I wake up. The job first ran on an 8 GB instance for about 2.5 cents, but Gemma peaked near 7.4 GiB there, so it moved to 16 GB for about a cent more per night.

From a script to an app

Around the pipeline, I built a FastAPI server and a React PWA:

  • My books, only for me. Sign-in goes through Auth0, the server checks every token, and books live in MongoDB Atlas tied to the verified account. Tests make sure one reader never sees another reader's books.
  • A library that looks like a book catalog, with covers from Open Library. When there's no reliable match, a book gets a plain placeholder instead of a guessed edition.
  • Adding a book, the lazy way. I type it or photograph the cover. OCR suggests the title and author, nothing is saved until I confirm, and the cover photo is never stored. Same rule as the quotes: the machine suggests, I decide.
  • Photos go to the night run, privately. From a book's page I photograph what I highlighted; the phone shrinks the photo and the server stores it in a private Cloudflare R2 bucket. The nightly job claims each pending page, writes its quotes with a small crop of the passage, and deletes the photo. If Gemma can't read a page, the photo waits for another night instead of settling for OCR alone.
  • The morning review. Each quote sits next to the crop it came from. I keep, edit or delete it, or add a passage the run missed; where OCR and Gemma disagreed, the app says so.
  • A careful PWA. Its service worker keeps only a public "you're offline" page. Sign-in data, books and photos never touch its cache.

What's still ahead

The full loop works: library, page capture, night run and morning review. Next come search by meaning across my quotes, the Notion export, deleting a book together with its quotes, and a dedicated in-app camera.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • My reading stays mine. My photos and highlights are read by a model running in my own night job, not sent to a third-party AI API.
  • It costs a few cents a night. A small open model on a plain CPU is cheap enough to run every night for years, with no per-request bill.
  • The model doesn't change under me. The whole design rests on knowing how Gemma fails. With the weights pinned in my image, tomorrow's model fails the same way today's does, so the checks I tuned against it keep working.
  • Swappable parts. The model and the OCR sit behind small interfaces, so a better open model can replace Gemma without touching the rest.

The Lazy Payoff

Before: in a dense book, I highlight 2 or 3 passages per page. Copying them is a 30 to 60 minute typing session, so I keep postponing it, and the quotes pile up in books I've already shelved.

After: one photo per highlighted page, taken while the book is still open, and a short review over breakfast. The review screen now exists, so I'll measure the real review time over the next books I read.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 e4b reads every highlighted block, cross-checked against OCR.
  • Best Use of Render: the nightly CPU cron job that runs the extraction.
  • Best Use of MongoDB Atlas: each reader's books, stored per verified account.
